title: Whose bias gets coded? Psychology's role in decolonizing AI
abstract: Who decides whose minds-and whose biases-get embedded in the algorithms that shape our world? The discipline of psychology, with its foundational assumptions and cultural biases, is deeply woven into artificial intelligence systems, influencing whose perspectives are valued and whose are marginalized. Bias in artificial intelligence is often described as a technical flaw, yet many of its origins are psychological-rooted in the constructs, methods, and epistemic values of psychology as a field. At the same time, bias also emerges from technical design choices, economic incentives, and governance structures. Our focus here is on psychology's distinctive role within this broader sociotechnical system (Ukanwa, 2024). This article argues that psychology both contributes to AI bias and holds unique potential to decolonize it through culturally inclusive design. To make this case, we first show how psychological constructs, often derived from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) contexts, have been embedded into AI in ways that amplify inequities. We then draw on decolonial traditions in psychology to propose standards and practices that could steer AI toward global representativeness, epistemic justice, and liberatory outcomes.Algorithms inherit ways of thinking that reflect Western-centric models of behaviour and identity (Rodier et al., 2023). Foundational critiques in AI ethics have already shown that models risk reproducing and amplifying social and cultural hierarchies, for instance uncover in the influential "stochastic parrots" argument that large-scale models inevitably encode representational harms (Bender et al., 2021).As machine learning models increasingly rely on psychological constructs such as decisionmaking, affect detection, and personality assessment in simulating or forecasting human behaviour, such constructs-frequently borrowed from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies-are universalized globally, often in spite of cultural specificity (Li et al., 2024;Peters & Carman, 2024). Recent empirical studies show that, in what ways language models possess not only linguistic but cultural and ideological biases as well, and we are forced to consider whose voices and perspectives they are representative of (Santurkar et al., 2023). Such a procedure makes the AI technologies instruments for the communication not only of wisdom but ideological imperatives, and brings to the fore pertinent questions regarding whose psychology gets encoded and at whose expense (Shukla, 2025). Calls for more pluralistic models of AI alignment (Sorensen et al., 2024) are accurate where such a procedure exists, but a decolonial lens expands our eye to awareness that what gets encoded is not only behaviour or cognitive processes but ideology, and brings with it the mandate for a psychological science realignment as a primary consideration in constructing ethically solidary, culturally inclusive technologies.Psychology did much in teaching us about bias, from the initial work of Kahneman and Tversky on heuristics to the most recent on implicit bias (Dominguez-Catena et al., 2025). Although this research has informed contemporary AI development, it has not proved sufficient to prevent the emergence and propagation of harmful biases in AI systems. We recognize, however, that bias is not always inherently negative; as recent work shows, certain forms of bias can be benign or even beneficial, while others entrench inequities (Hagendorff & Fabi, 2024;Waters & Honenberger, 2025). Our focus in this article is on those biases that reproduce systemic disadvantage and cultural exclusion.A classic example is in facial recognition technology employed in Detroit, where in 2023 the system misclassified Black faces five to ten times more often than white faces (Basheer, 2024). The imbalance is traced to training sets dominated by Caucasian facial features and to psychological assumptions-such as the idea that emotions are universally expressed and recognized across all cultures-that do not account for cultural and phenotypic differences (Domnich & Anbarjafari, 2021). The National Institute of Standards and Technology confirmed these findings, reporting racial disparities in 189 algorithms developed by 99 different companies (Grother et al., 2019) Similarly, Amazon's defunct recruitment algorithm penalized resumes containing keywords such as 'women's chess club' or references to all-female colleges. The system reproduced historical gender biases embedded in its training data, effectively privileging male-coded language and experiences. While not a psychological mechanism per se, this outcome parallels attribution errors studied in psychology, where competence is inferred through biased cues, and illustrates how data-driven systems can replicate structural inequities (Mahapatra & Mujtaba, 2019;Venkateshwaran, 2025).These cases illustrate how psychological constructs, when uncritically embedded into AI, can entrench and even amplify social inequities. The preceding examples underscore how psychological constructs, when uncritically implemented, amplify inequities. But this raises a critical question: is all bias inherently harmful? Some scholars argue that the goal of "bias-free AI" is both unattainable and misleading, since all models reflect values, assumptions, and standpoints (Fabi & Hagendorff, n.d.).The key issue is not whether bias exists, but whether it is reflexively acknowledged, equitably distributed, and aligned with principles of justice.From a decolonial perspective, the distinction lies between biases that "punch down" (reinforcing domination and exclusion) and those that "punch up" (resisting oppression and amplifying marginalized voices). Decolonial psychology traditions-from Fanon's analyses of colonial subjectivity (Fanon, 1967) to Martín-Baró's liberation psychology (Martín-Baró, 1994) and Indigenous frameworks of relationality emphasizing interconnectedness and collective well-being (Wilson, 2008)-remind us that partiality can serve emancipatory ends when it surfaces silenced knowledge systems rather than suppressing them.This article therefore rejects the ideal of "bias-free AI" in favour of a normative standard: AI systems must disclose their epistemic commitments, embrace cultural pluralism, and actively counter oppressive hierarchies. In practice, this means building technologies that recognize the inevitability of bias, while steering it toward inclusivity, accountability, and justice.The issue of bias in AI is not only technical but also connected to the long history of colonialism in psychology-pathologizing native cultures, medicalizing difference, and exporting Western diagnostic guidelines as if they were universal (Deva et al., 2025). Such epistemological biases are perpetually integrated into AI technologies. For example, the talk therapy conversational bots Wysa and Woebot, developed almost entirely from Western clinical databases, incorrectly interpreted culturally characteristic Indian expressions. A 2024 study identified that Indian users' statements such as "family pressure is my karma" were pathologized as depressive symptoms, deserving of unsuitable therapeutic interventions (Viberg et al., 2023). Generative models such as Midjourney and DALL-E also incorrectly represented Indian subcultures: a 2024 University of Pennsylvania study noted that the prompt "Indian family dinner" produced poverty-related images 73% of the time, while "American family dinner" produced middle-class settings.These are described as psychological assumptions because they draw directly from psychological constructs-such as the universality of diagnostic categories (e.g., DSMbased criteria for distress), standardized measures of emotion, and Western notions of family and identity-that have historically been treated as objective and culture-free. When transferred into AI systems, such constructs enact a second-order colonization: exporting Western norms while erasing non-Western modalities of being under the guise of objectivity and universality (Ghosh et al., 2024;Kumar et al., 2025).Psychology can help repair these damages by fostering epistemic pluralism, co-design, and critical reflexivity. One strong example comes from South Africa, where researchers collaborated with Zulu communities to co-design a tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis algorithm. In Zulu, the idiom "isifuba sibuhlungu" literally means "the chest is painful," but it carries cultural and linguistic nuances that early English-trained diagnostic systems failed to interpret correctly. Because these AI models were trained only on biomedical descriptions in English, they initially misclassified the condition, lowering diagnostic accuracy to 68%. By incorporating Zulu terminology and involving community members in the design process, accuracy improved dramatically to 92%. This shows that co-design not only raises technical precision but also affirms the legitimacy of local knowledge in medical AI.There is a similar lesson from Aotearoa/New Zealand, in which Māori researchers established the Te Hiku voice model as an embodiment of the speaking voice of te reo Māori.Off-the-shelf commercial speech-recognition software had an error rate of as high as 47% among Māori speakers directly because they were excluded from international training datasets. By collating and controlling their own data sets, Māori communities brought errors to near zero while keeping their voices and the way they are stored in sovereign hands. The project proves that Indigenous-driven design is both feasible in terms of system performance increase and in terms of cultural sovereignty protection.These exemplars conform with the new GPA guidelines (Global Psychology Alliance, 2023), that emphasize three practices: cultural disclosure, cross-validation, and site-based audits.Cultural disclosure obliges researchers to be transparent in marking the cultural heritage of their data so that Western constructs will cease being presented as universal. Crossvalidation over three or more settings demands that psychological constructs and AI models be proved in diverse cultural settings rather than in WEIRD populations so that they can be applied more widely. Site-based audits demand independent, often community-based examination of psychological research and applications of AI so that ethical propriety as well as cultural sensibility may be established.Applied to AI, these standards mean that therapeutic chatbots, diagnostic algorithms, or predictive models should (1) disclose the cultural provenance of their training data, (2) undergo validation in multiple culturally distinct populations, and (3) be audited by independent panels that include community stakeholders. Together, these measures shift psychology from passive collaborator in bias to active ethical design architect, embedding justice and cultural pluralism into the development of AI (Masaka, 2019;Ofosu-Asare, 2024).The question of whose bias gets coded necessarily opens onto the complicity of psychology in the empowerment of systems that disguise ideology as objectivity. The examples-from the Dutch tax algorithm's racial bias through Chicago's predictive policing-are used here just to illustrate how psychological inventions, disguised under the pretence of universal laws, have themselves been used to encode the colonial relations of power in AI. Not the predestined product of technology but the product of political and disciplinary choices, they may be undone through the decentralized production of knowledge through both crosscultural validation as well as community co-design. Cross-cultural validation and community co-design are related but distinct processes: validation demonstrates that a model's performance is not WEIRD-restricted, while co-design ensures the model is legitimate, safe, and valuable in a specific cultural setting. Epistemic responsibility must draw sustenance also from independent data and algorithmic audits. Such audits must take place under the aegis of cross-disciplinary working groups of academic specialists, civic societies, and citizens from communities most at risk of the effects of AI. Their remit is in technical proficiency as well as in representational democracy, such that fairness, cultural compatibility, and transparency must be taken into account in many different lexicons. Justice must become an organizing principle both in the generation and in use of AI. Psychology is at a fork in the road at present: it can become an architecture of exclusion, or become the scaffold for liberation through the generation of culturally compatible and ethically informed systems of AI. The code, and the effects of code, are ours to rewrite.

title: Catalyzing research-enabled clinical practice: What everyone can do
abstract: “Without data, you’re just another person with an opinion.” –W. Edwards Deming In the evolving landscape of clinical practice, every patient encounter represents a potential contribution to scientific discovery. Yet, individual clinician experiences often do not translate into published evidence. So, there is an obvious need for practitioners to assume the dual roles of healthcare provider and knowledge creator. This transformative journey should begin as a self-driven change starting within every practitioner who desires to become a contributor, not just a consumer of scientific evidence. Upgrading ophthalmic clinics to research-enabled spaces can transform even modest practices into hubs of data-driven publication, thus democratizing clinical research. This editorial proposes a practical five-step framework to engage, equip, and empower clinician–researchers to integrate research habits, skills, and infrastructure within everyday ophthalmic practice. STEP 1: INITIATE THE HABIT OF REGULAR SCIENTIFIC READING The first step toward nurturing a research-enabled practice culture is cultivating the habit of regular scientific reading. Integrating short, focused reading sessions and dedicated reading time into daily work schedules encourages reflective practice, enhances clinical reasoning, facilitates evidence-based decision-making, and nurtures curiosity-driven inquiry—the bedrock of clinician-led research. Many Journals are now open access which means readers have free access to a large body of online scientific content, including short summaries and CME-linked updates, to support busy practitioners in keeping pace with emerging knowledge.[1,2] Case reports and photograph essays are a good place for beginners to start engaging seriously with scientific publications without being intimidated by statistical and research jargon. Regular reading of peer reviewed indexed journals also provides practitioners with valuable insights into contemporary publication trends and requirements, thus enabling identification of research gaps in their own practices, sparking independent investigations. STEP 2: GET FAMILIAR WITH RESEARCH METHODOLOGY BASICS Understanding the fundamentals of research methodology empowers clinicians to transform clinical observations into publishable scientific output. Key competencies include proficiency in using search engines and databases (PubMed, Scopus, Embase), manuscript writing and referencing tools (Mendeley, Zotero, EndNote), and data management and biostatistics software (SPSS, R, Jamovi). Equally important are sound principles of research ethics, including informed consent, data anonymization, and compliance with institutional review board (IRB) norms. With the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) in research, clinicians are increasingly leveraging AI-driven tools for literature mapping (e.g., Research Rabbit, Elicit), automated referencing, and statistical assistance. Upskilling opportunities are plenty through workshops by academic institutions, instructional courses at conferences, and online, self-paced learning resources (e.g., The Elsevier Researcher Academy, Clinical Research Methodology in Ophthalmology series, Museum of the Eye Research and Resources from the American Academy of Ophthalmology). Webinars such as Publish and Flourish (IJO–KJO) and mentorship programs by Harvard, AAO, and Women in Ophthalmology (WIO) offer structured pathways for clinician–researchers to refine these essential skills.[3-6] STEP 3: ACQUIRE CLINICAL DOCUMENTATION AND OPHTHALMIC IMAGING SKILLS In ophthalmology, where disease expression and response to therapy are primarily visual, documentation extends far beyond written records. A research-enabled clinic should emphasize systematic capture, storage, and standardization of ocular photographs and imaging data. This includes fundus photography, slit-lamp imaging, anterior segment videos, and OCT scans, all of which contribute longitudinal visual data for both patient care and research. For clinician–researchers, mastering basic ophthalmic photography and image quality control is essential. This includes understanding illumination, focus, magnification, and image labeling standards to ensure reproducibility. Smartphone-based ophthalmic photography has revolutionized accessibility, enabling high-quality imaging in resource-limited settings. Low-cost devices [Table 1], such as Remidio Fundus on Phone (FOP), Phelcom Eyer, oDocs Nun, and D-EYE, allow retinal and anterior segment imaging with minimal training and cost.[7-9] Even simple DIY slit-lamp adapters using 3D-printed mounts can transform routine examinations into documented datasets. Academic institutions and resource rich practices may adopt integration with digital platforms and Cloud-based EMRs that further support secure image storage, annotation, and retrieval. Training opportunities in ophthalmic imaging, AI-assisted image analysis, and data anonymization are widely available through the skill transfer courses and workshops by professional bodies like AAO, AIOS, and other academic institutions. The goal for every aspiring clinical researcher, regardless of their practice setting, should be to upskill themselves in this respect to build a research-ready visual archive that fuels both clinical excellence and scientific discovery.Table 1: Low-cost ophthalmic imaging and documentation toolsSTEP 4: UPGRADE YOUR CLINIC TO A RESEARCH-READY SPACE Building a research-ready clinical space requires integrating data systems, workflows, and processes that support ethical and efficient research. Essential elements include standardized data collection templates, secure cloud storage compliant with privacy regulations, and well-defined data retrieval systems. Clinics can adopt electronic health record (EHR) systems with research modules or structured data fields for automated export into spreadsheets or analytics tools. Maintaining a research logbook—digital or paper-based—helps track study ideas, ongoing data collection, and outcomes. Creating this environment does not demand a large budget; it demands clarity and sense of purpose. Even small clinics can establish secure digital folders, assign basic roles for data entry, and use free project management tools (e.g., Notion, Trello, Google Workspace) for coordination. When such processes are normalized, clinical spaces become continuous engines of research—each patient encounter contributing to a growing body of practice-based evidence. STEP 5: DEVELOP SOFT SKILLS FOR NETWORKING, COLLABORATION, AND COMMUNICATION Clinical research thrives in collaborative ecosystems. Developing soft skills, particularly in communication, teamwork, and networking is vital for initiating partnerships and sharing ideas. Practitioners from outside academia have a lot to gain from finding and actively collaborating with likeminded research partners in academic institutions and centers of excellence having a robust research culture. Online platforms, like ResearchGate, LinkedIn, and ONE Network, enable clinicians to engage in scholarly discussions, access global resources, and seek coauthors or mentors. Participation in professional societies fosters opportunities for multicenter collaboration. Effective communication also extends to scientific writing and conference presentations, where clarity and persuasion determine impact. As clinician–researchers gain visibility, they contribute not only to science but also to development of a supportive culture of inquiry within their own institutions.[10,11] CONCLUSION Democratizing clinical research begins by nurturing scientific temper, clinical curiosity, and research skill enhancement in practitioners, irrespective of their practice settings. Further, transforming clinical spaces into research-ready environments embodies the philosophy that scientific discovery should not be confined to academic centers alone but should thrive wherever patients are being cared for. By adopting a five pronged action plan of regular scientific reading, foundational research training, ophthalmic imaging documentation, incorporating structured data workflow systems in practice and collaborative networking, clinicians engaged in patient care can generating high-quality, practice-based evidence. These step-by-step, deliberate shifts in research culture to include individual clinician experiences can collectively accelerate the global movement toward equitable, evidence-based ophthalmic practice. This editorial also marks my swansong and this issue, the final act of the current editorial team. Serving as Editor-in-Chief over the past two years has been a deeply gratifying, intellectually stimulating, and enriching experience. These years of focused effort have been marked by significant progress, reflected in the following KJO initiatives: Publication of six issues of KJO, including a focus issue on Glaucoma Introduction of more than a dozen new sections in the journal Research to Reality: A themed webinar series on evidence-based ophthalmic practice Two KJO sessions on research empowerment at Drishti KJO Online Quiz Series KJO Flash Cards A dedicated KJO channel on the KSOS website Launch of Digital KJO Introduction of KJO Appreciation Awards for outstanding reviewers and the most prolific author It has been a privilege to contribute to the academic growth of our fraternity through these initiatives. I express my sincere gratitude to Dr. Thomas Cherian (President, KSOS 2023–24) for the opportunity to serve, and thank Dr Mahesh. G (President, KSOS 2024-25) and the KSOS team for all support extended. I am also indebted to our esteemed emeritus editors, Dr Sudha. V and Dr Smita Narayan, for their invaluable guidance. My sincere appreciation to Dr. Sujith Nayanar, KSOS website editor, whose seamless collaboration was instrumental in the success of many digital initiatives, particularly the KJO channel. I wholeheartedly thank Dr Praveen Nirmalan for his valuable contributions to the webinar series and related academic activities. Finally, I acknowledge the efforts of my remarkable editorial team and appreciate their energy, commitment, and dedicated efforts which have made KJO grow from strength to strength. As I step down from the role of Editor-in-Chief, I do so with a smile on my lips and a song in my heart, knowing that I have given our journal my very best and, hopefully, left a few lasting imprints upon its hallowed pages. The future of KJO shines bright—I wish the incoming Editor and her team every success in taking this journal to even greater heights.

title: Historians: from manuscript to machine learning
abstract: 1. Introduction: Historians have consistently adapted their methodologies to the available technological tools, progressing from manual examination of manuscripts to the use of advanced machine learning-based instruments. Early modern historians employed manual techniques to create, collect, and analyze handwritten manuscripts and literary sources found in archives, libraries, private collections, and government records, thereby reconstructing historical events. The invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century fundamentally transformed historical study and writing. Subsequent innovations, including typewriters and microfilm, significantly altered the processes of recording, preserving, and disseminating historical information. In the late twentieth century, the advent of computers initiated a digital revolution that redefined the sources, techniques, and epistemologies of historical research. Computers allowed historians to organize and analyze source materials with unprecedented precision (Alves 2014). Recent advances in machine learning have further accelerated this transformation, enabling the analysis of large-scale digital data. This study examines the evolving relationship between technological innovation and historical practice, from handwritten manuscripts to machine learning. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how technological advancements shape historical thought and methodology. 2. Sub-sections: 2.1. Pre digital age: 2.1.1. Printing Press Before the advent of the printing press, historians manually copied manuscripts, which limited access to historical documents and confined research to a select, elite audience primarily focused on religious subjects. For instance, the Venerable Bede's monastic chronicles reinforced prevailing religious views, while the Epic of Gilgamesh demonstrated the scarcity and variety of preserved accounts. Consequently, historical narratives largely described and supported established beliefs, with minimal critical analysis. The arrival of the printing press democratized access to books and significantly changed the nature and scope of historical scholarship (Curtius 1990). The printing press expanded historical research by facilitating the production of sources. While handwritten documents were exclusive, printed works became more affordable and accurate due to reduced errors (Eisenstein 1980). This change promoted secular and comparative perspectives. Increased accessibility enabled historians like Edward Gibbon (Gibbon et al. 1776) and François Guizot (Cave 2000) to approach history with greater analytical rigor, fostering the development of professional historiography. Print technology improved source criticism and citation. Scholars debated document reliability and separated authentic records from forgeries. Print made critical analysis more accessible, as with the work of Scaliger and Bodin (Grafton 1993). Texts by Bede and Biondo inspired interest in classical narratives (Kelley 1998). The scale of book production led to the establishment of professional historians and archives, despite some resistance. These innovations set the stage for the development of scientific historiography. Despite enhanced accessibility and methodological advancement achieved through print technology, the exclusion of diverse groups persisted. Marginalized perspectives—including those of women, indigenous peoples, and colonial subjects—were frequently omitted. This exclusion highlights the continuing imperative for inclusivity in historical scholarship. Published narratives that foregrounded established viewpoints often reflected prevailing social biases, thereby limiting the representation of alternative voices. However, collective efforts gradually increased the visibility of some previously marginalized accounts, such as those associated with slaves, colonial subjects, and the women' s suffrage movement. When more records were printed and standardized, historians could compare the same editions more easily. This improvement led to enhanced accuracy and consistency in research (Eisenstein 1980; McKeown 2021). Evidence-based analysis and reliability became more common. Earlier methods, such as oral traditions, still offer valuable information that print may miss. The print era introduced new tools, such as pagination and indexes, which made research more systematic and efficient. These developments created the foundation for today's critical approaches to history (Serjeantson 2006). 2.1.2. Typewriter The typewriter and microfilm improved efficiency and helped establish archival standards. The widespread adoption of the typewriter allowed for faster dissemination and clearer presentation of scholarly ideas, influencing both the teaching and understanding of history (Adler 2023). The typewriter's mechanical process increased productivity by generating legible text more quickly. Typed manuscripts enabled clearer peer evaluation and scrutiny, which strengthened scholarly standards (Roy 2021). The introduction of the typewriter thus improved the speed, readability, and consistency of historical writing, further formalizing the field. These technological developments redefined not only historians' workflows but also the perceived authority and objectivity of historical scholarship. For example, historians such as Charles Beard produced comprehensive analyses with greater efficiency, marking a transition in the economic interpretation of history. Standardizing text with the typewriter encouraged professionalism and empirical study, but could obscure subjective interpretation. Documents seen as objective are influenced by historians' choices; narrative emphasis or selective quoting may sway interpretation. Thus, personal bias persists within seemingly objective writing. However, In both colonial and postcolonial contexts, the standardization imposed by the typewriter often reinforced existing class and gender hierarchies (Fine 1993; Chung 2022). Access to typewriters was generally confined to privileged social strata due to its high cost (Gitelman 2000) and their professional use frequently mirrored prevailing power dynamics, notably in contexts where women were predominantly relegated to clerical positions (England and Boyer 2009). In addition to technological developments, the social norms associated with writing evolved in response to the typewriter. Initially, mechanical writing was perceived as less personal than handwriting, which was seen as conveying sincerity and refinement. Over time, the typewritten word became a marker of professionalism and formal expertise. This evolution illustrates that historical knowledge relies not only on empirical evidence but also on the changing relationship between scholars and their tools. The typewriter fostered an aura of objectivity and authority, while its standardization sometimes obscured interpretive subjectivity, thereby shaping the boundaries of historiographical practice. 2.2. Early Digital Age 2.2.1 Microfilm: In the early twentieth century, microfilm technology, a precursor to mass digitization (Milligan 2022), fundamentally restructured preservation and access to sources (Binkley 1936). Developed by John Dancer (Luther 1959) and further improved by Rene Dagron (Luther 1996), microfilm reduced the size of materials for efficient storage and aimed to stabilize fragile documents. It played a crucial role in debates concerning archival access, as it enabled unprecedented opportunities for historians to access rare and geographically dispersed materials. Microfilm enabled researchers to access documents without the need for travel, making rare records more widely available. In the 1930s, institutions began microfilming projects to increase global access to manuscripts (Foster 1985). Microfilm and foundational digital practices greatly expanded access and transformed historical research. By making previously inaccessible materials available, microfilm widened research possibilities. Digitization amplified this shift, enabling analysis on a larger scale with greater complexity. Contemporary digitization, with frameworks like International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF), prioritizes metadata to systematically enhance access and engagement. These developments reshaped historical research by supporting data-driven methods and highlighting technology as an active force in the evolution of the discipline. Nevertheless, despite these advancements in access, microfilm was mainly limited to select institutions and required specialized equipment. Navigating collections was slow, highlighting the eventual need for digital transformation. Digital databases later addressed these issues by simplifying document search and retrieval, vastly improving research efficiency and access. However, this phase of digitization is not without its challenges. Issues such as digital preservation, data loss risks, and access inequalities have emerged, prompting ongoing discussions on how to ensure equitable access while securing digital records for future generations. 2.3. Digital age: Punch cards (early data storage cards) revolutionized data storage and enabled quantitative analysis in the 1950s, leading historians and social scientists to adopt computational methods. Roberto Busa pioneered the application of digital technology in the humanities with the creation of Index Thomisticus, a computational analysis of Thomas Aquinas's works (Fantoli 2023; Sula and Hill 2019; Rockwell and Passarotti 2019). These early innovations marked the beginning of a profound transformation: digital technologies would fundamentally reshape how historians access information, conduct research, and interpret the past. Following these foundational developments, mainframe computers—such as the IBM 1401 and UNIVAC—enabled large-scale data analysis. This advance sparked the cliometric revolution, which used quantitative, or numerical, techniques in the study of history. Tools like SPSS, a statistical analysis program, let scholars reinterpret historical narratives using empirical, data-driven approaches. Frank and Harriet Owsley (1949) used quantitative methods to study Southern social patterns. Building on this, from the 1960s, computers reshaped global historical research. Researchers such as Robert Fogel, Stanley Engerman, and Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie applied digital techniques to historical records. Since 2000, digital libraries—collections of digitized resources online—have further enhanced access and research methods. As the field advanced, historians witnessed transformative effects. Technology provided access to millions of documents and artifacts online, enabling remote research (Gomes and Costa 2014). Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and data mining uncover patterns and encourage collaboration with programmers. Notably, the Valley of the Shadow project (1993) applies GIS to examine two communities during the American Civil War (Thomas and Ayers 2003). Interactive media and digital storytelling—exemplified by the Digital History Project—bolster public engagement and revitalize historical narratives. This shift also unfolded in phases as computers integrated into historical research. In the initial stage, historians converted source information into structured datasets by encoding facts, dates, names, and events from documents, such as census records, into databases. For instance, population studies digitized census data for easier analysis. With digital foundations established, historians entered a second phase, where they analyzed datasets, identified patterns, tested hypotheses, and uncovered language changes using linguistic software (Hendrickx and Marquilhas 2011). Computers produced new insights—graphs, tables, dictionaries. These methods fostered specialized fields. As these methods became central, digital technologies have significantly altered the nature, accessibility, and volume of historical sources. As Timothy Hitchcock states, "The digital archive has changed the nature of the historical record" ("DHLU 2013 Symposium (Luxembourg, 5 December 2013) — Keynote: Tim Hitchcock - CVCE Website," n.d.) Previously inaccessible manuscripts, newspapers, and records are now available online, allowing historians to use vast datasets. Projects like the Old Bailey Online exemplify how digitisation reshapes the materiality of sources by offering searchable access to 197,000 trials, a scale previously unimaginable ("Old Bailey Proceedings Online (Www.Oldbaileyonline.Org), 1674–1913. - Google Search," n.d.). Similarly, the Transcribe Bentham project demonstrates how collaborative digital initiatives have expanded participation in both the creation of and access to historical documents; volunteers transcribe manuscripts, making primary sources widely available and accelerating research progress (Causer and Terras 2014). Despite enhanced access, the use of digital surrogates, while offering accessibility, raises questions about authenticity and the material context of original documents. As Johanna Drucker notes, "Digitised materials are not facsimiles but interpretations" (Drucker 2013), highlighting how the transformation of physical sources into digital formats introduces a new layer of mediation. Alongside these challenges, technologies influence methods and methodology, especially through digital humanities tools for quantitative analysis, text mining, and GIS mapping. For example, historians use Voyant Tools for textual analysis (Bradley 2012; Nyhan et al. 2023) and GIS for spatial history (Da Silveira 2014). Yet, Ian Milligan argues the "methodological shift is secondary to the fundamental change in the source base itself" (Milligan 2019). Methodology changes in response to the transformed materiality and scale of digital sources, not as a standalone transformation. Digital tools enable quantitative analysis on an unprecedented scale. Network analysis and visualisation tools offer new ways to examine patterns, relationships, and trends across vast corpora. For example, the "Mining the Dispatch" project utilizes topic modeling to explore themes in Civil War newspapers, uncovering insights that are difficult to find manually. Digital history also encourages interdisciplinary methods, blending historical inquiry with data science, linguistics, and geography. This convergence challenges traditional methodology, pushing historians to engage with new epistemologies and reconsider notions of evidence, interpretation, and narrative. This global digital progression exhibits stark regional contrasts, reflecting differences in priorities, strategies, and challenges. In India, digitization efforts focus on preserving diverse community records in multiple languages, aiming to address the country's significant linguistic diversity; however, these efforts are often constrained by limited infrastructure and resources (Chowdhary 2024). In Southeast Asia, by contrast, state-run projects in countries like Vietnam and Indonesia often prioritize official narratives, restricting alternative or community perspectives. Latin America offers a contrasting, community-driven approach: projects in Peru and Argentina, such as Archivo Memoria Abierta, prioritize indigenous and social histories, representing a "bottom-up" model distinct from the state-centered strategies seen elsewhere. Kenya and other African countries present another contrast: their digitization initiatives emphasize building digital infrastructure and safeguarding historical materials. Despite limited funding, these efforts expand access and focus on long-term preservation. For example, the Digitization of Africa's Cultural Heritage (DACH) project targets the preservation of Kenyan archives for future generations. This strategy, centered on infrastructure and heritage protection, contrasts with regions that prioritize content diversity or dominant narratives (Ndegwa et al. 2022; Aldirdiri 2024; Musembe et al. 2025). Europe and North America provide a further contrast, characterized by robust infrastructure, advanced analytics, and handling of complex datasets. These regions typically prioritize major languages, sometimes at the expense of less widely spoken ones (Ahnert et al. 2023). Their strategies focus on maximizing analytical capability and data access, but risks persist: lost context, technological obsolescence, and training gaps remain, necessitating sustained collaboration. Juxtaposing these regions with others reveals how policy orientation, language priorities, and resource allocation create distinctly state-driven, community-centered, or analytics-focused approaches to digital history. Despite differences in approach, these regional digitization strategies have a direct impact on historical research by shaping the accessibility and interpretation of information. Advanced infrastructure enables high-level analysis and diverse narratives, whereas areas with resource constraints may face challenges in accessing and preserving information. This global diversity enriches historical research and showcases regional adaptation to technological opportunities. In addition to research practices, digital media have also transformed the communication of historical research. Open-access platforms now reach broader audiences, while projects feature interactive maps, timelines, and videos. Social media and online forums expedite scholarly communication and foster academic communities. These global developments demonstrate that digital methods now define historical research by reshaping sources, interpretation, and engagement. Technology's influence is not just technical but methodological, fundamentally changing how historians access information and construct knowledge about the past. title: From Barbers to Bots: A Surgeon’s Odyssey
abstract: INTRODUCTION Surgery, a field involving physical intervention to treat diseases, has a history as ancient as humanity. From the primitive procedures of early civilizations to the advanced, minimally invasive techniques of the modern era, surgery has undergone significant transformations. Over the centuries, its scope, complexity, precision, and effectiveness have expanded. This article provides a comprehensive historical perspective on the evolution of surgery, tracing its development from ancient times, through the medieval and Renaissance periods, to modern advancements, highlighting key innovations and important moments that have profoundly impacted human health and disease treatment. HUMBLE BEGINNINGS: THE EARLY AGES The earliest evidence of surgery dates back to ancient civilizations such as Athens, Rome, Egypt, China, and Alexandria. Trepanation or burr hole surgery was likely the first surgical procedure, with skulls excavated in France dating to 6500 BCE showing trepanation holes.[1] The ancient Egyptians practiced circumcision, and the Ebers Papyrus (1550 BCE) mentions treatments for burns, animal bites, and abscesses.[2] Engravings of ancient surgical tools are found in Kom Ombo, Egypt, and the Edwin Smith Papyrus details trauma procedures, sutures, and wound management.[3] Sushruta, an ancient Indian surgeon, described his techniques in the Sushruta Samhita, including rhinoplasty, which is still practiced today. He worked in Kasi (Varanasi) between 1200 and 600 BCE.[4] Greek physician Hippocrates outlined methods for fracture reduction, hemorrhoid treatment, and head injury care in the Hippocratic Corpus.[5] Alexandrian surgeons such as Celsus and Galen contributed to ligatures, hernia, and ophthalmic surgeries, bone reduction techniques, and the use of Mandrake as an anesthetic. Galen’s four principles included observation, writing, dissection, and the theory of the four humors.[6] Ancient Chinese surgeon Hua Tao used anesthesia around 140–208 Anno Domini (AD), and Bian Que reportedly performed heart transplants around 300 BCE.[7] Al-Zahrawi, a prominent Arab surgeon around 900 AD, authored the “Kitab al-Tasrif,” detailing surgical procedures from dentistry to child delivery. He insisted that only those with extensive knowledge of anatomy and physiology should practice surgery, a view later adopted by Halsted in surgical residency programs.[8] During the Renaissance, Ambroise Paré, a French army surgeon, introduced ligatures to stop bleeding instead of cauterization and advocated gentle wound treatment, improving surgical outcomes significantly.[9] THE DARK AGES: MEDIEVAL TIMES The foundation laid by ancient surgeons was largely lost in the early medieval period, with surgery devolving into practice often indistinguishable from butchery. Performed mostly by barbers, these practitioners, known as barber surgeons, were common in England. Local religious practices overshadowed scientific knowledge, resulting in a significant decline in surgical quality and safety. The risk of death from surgical interventions was considered higher than battlefield dangers. Surgery was sidelined by elite physicians, poor remuneration, filthy working conditions, lack of training, and biased surgical ethos.[10] The constant wars and changing geopolitical landscape necessitated skilled individuals to manage war wounds, leading to the emergence of brilliant surgeons who revived and transformed the discipline. Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), in his treatise “De Humanis Corporis Fabrica,” described the anatomical basis of surgical practice and promoted “learning by dissecting yourself,” the earliest concept of hands-on training. His work in human dissection laid the foundation for modern anatomy and significantly improved the understanding of the human body, crucial for surgical advancement.[11] Ambroise Paré, a French army surgeon (1530–1590), revolutionized wound treatment by introducing emollients and ligating blood vessels for hemostasis instead of cauterizing with boiling oil. Paré’s humane and innovative approach significantly improved surgical outcomes and reduced patient suffering.[9] Despite these advancements, surgery was hampered by the lack of anesthesia and asepsis. Procedures were often performed in the open with multiple assistants pinning patients down. Survivors of the procedure often succumbed to infections due to the lack of aseptic techniques and proper postoperative care. The absence of adequate training contributed to the perception of surgery as a blind science fraught with risks and uncertainties.[2] The slow progress in surgical practices during medieval times underscores the critical importance of scientific inquiry and rigorous training in medicine. It was not until later centuries, with the introduction of anesthesia and asepsis, that surgery became a safer and more precise discipline, laying the groundwork for modern surgical practices. FOUNDATION OF MODERN SURGERY John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon, laid the scientific foundation for modern surgery through his experimental work. He created museum housing over 13,000 human specimens, which he used for detailed observation and analysis. Hunter’s work included innovative methods for dealing with aneurysmal arteries and enhancing the understanding of infection and inflammation. His systematic approach and dedication to empirical research significantly advanced surgical practice. Other important figures this era include Percival Pott, who identified the link between chimney sweep exposure and scrotal cancer and described tuberculosis of the spine, and Sir Astley Paston Cooper, who made substantial contributions to surgical anatomy.[12,13] The discovery of anesthesia marked a monumental milestone in surgery. Dr. Crawford Williamson Long first used ether as an anesthetic during the resection of a neck tumor, but William T.G. Morton, in 1846, successfully demonstrated the anesthetic properties of ether during a public dental procedure.[14] This revolutionized surgery by allowing complex and lengthy operations without pain. The discovery of curare, a muscle relaxant, further expanded surgical capabilities, enabling controlled, and safe procedures. Ether remained a primary anesthetic agent until more advanced and safer alternatives were developed.[15] The battle against surgical infections represented the next hurdle. Austrian obstetrician Ignaz Semmelweiss pioneered handwashing to prevent puerperal fever, initially met with skepticism but eventually accepted as a cornerstone of infection control. Joseph Lister, inspired by Louis Pasteur’s germ theory, introduced carbolic acid as a sterilizing agent for surgical instruments and wounds.[16,17] Lister’s antiseptic techniques drastically reduced postoperative infections, setting the stage for modern aseptic methods. Sir William Stewart Halsted formalized surgical training and introduced residency programs, emphasizing rigorous training, extensive knowledge of human anatomy, and meticulous surgical technique. Halsted pioneered several surgeries, including radical mastectomy for breast cancer, herniotomy, and innovative approaches to thyroid and vascular surgeries. He also introduced surgical gloves, improving hygiene, and enhancing surgeons’ dexterity and precision.[18,19] These developments in the scientific foundation, anesthesia, and antiseptic techniques propelled surgery forward, laying the groundwork for the remarkable progress that transformed surgery into a highly skilled and precise medical discipline.[20] AMALGAMATION OF SCIENCE AND ART: ERA OF LAPAROSCOPY AND ENDOSCOPY The introduction of laparoscopy and endoscopy revolutionized surgery by challenging the notion that “big surgeons give big incisions.” Advances in optics and digital technology led to the development of modern endoscopes, enabling complex procedures through small incisions.[21] This shift reduced patient recovery times, minimized scarring, and lowered complication risks. Kurt Semm pioneered laparoscopic surgery, developing various tools, and performing the first laparoscopic appendectomy in 1980.[22] Despite initial resistance, his persistence led to the widespread acceptance of laparoscopic techniques. Professional societies such as the Surgical Study Group on Endoscopy and Ultrasound (CAES) in Germany and the Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons in the U.S. played crucial roles in promoting these techniques.[23] Publications such as “Surgical Endoscopy” facilitated knowledge dissemination, training, and research. By the 1990s, laparoscopic cholecystectomy had become the gold standard for treating gallstone disease.[24] The success of this procedure demonstrated the efficacy and safety of laparoscopic techniques, leading to their adoption in various surgical fields. Advances in endoscopic technology, including high-definition cameras and sophisticated instruments, enabled surgeons to perform intricate procedures with greater precision. John E.A. Wickham, a British urologist, established a minimally invasive surgery department at the Institute of Urology in London, marking a significant milestone in formal endoscopic training.[25] Innovations such as cold light video endoscopy and charged coupled devices for high-definition imaging further fuelled enthusiasm for these techniques. The start of the 21st century saw the amalgamation of science, art, and technology in shaping the future of surgery. The era of “big surgeons-big incisions” was replaced by minimally invasive surgery principles.[26] Laparoscopic cholecystectomy served as a model, leading to significant advancements in bariatric, colorectal, and gynecological surgery. A study conducted between 2008 and 2012 revealed increased use of laparoscopic techniques in major U.S. teaching hospitals, with high adoption rates for bariatric surgery (94%), appendectomy (79.2%), cholecystectomy (77.1%), colectomy (52.4%), ventral hernia repair (28.1%), and rectal resection (18.3%).[27] This trend highlighted the growing acceptance and preference for minimally invasive approaches. ERA OF ROBOTIC SURGERY The concept of remote surgery, pioneered by the US military and Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, aimed at providing advanced surgical care in combat zones without immediate evacuation. This led to the development of early surgical robots such as automated endoscopic system for optimal positioning and ZEUS robotic surgical system, which combined laparoscopic techniques with robotic technology.[28] These systems laid the groundwork for integrating robotics into surgical practice. Intuitive Surgical’s Da Vinci Surgical System marked a significant advancement in robotic surgery, offering improved instrument exchange, stereoscopic vision, and enhanced patient safety.[29] It allowed surgeons to perform complex procedures with greater precision and control using a high-definition, three-dimensional (3D) view, and robotic arms equipped with wristed instruments, mimicking human dexterity with enhanced stability. Robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy became a widely used application of the Da Vinci system, offering superior outcomes compared to traditional open surgery, such as reduced blood loss, less postoperative pain, shorter hospital stays, and quicker recovery times.[30] This success paved the way for adopting robotic systems in various specialties, including gynecology, cardiothoracic surgery, and general surgery. Robotic surgery’s precision and minimally invasive nature made it suitable for delicate procedures requiring meticulous tissue handling. Advancements in technology, like haptic feedback, allowed surgeons to sense tissue texture and resistance, enhancing precision.[31] Advanced imaging techniques, such as fluorescence imaging, improved visualization of anatomical structures and critical areas such as blood vessels and nerves. Significant investments in research and innovation from governmental and private sectors drove robotic surgery development. Companies like Intuitive Surgical refined and expanded their systems’ capabilities, making them more accessible and versatile.[32] Consequently, robotic surgery use has grown exponentially, with many hospitals worldwide adopting these technologies to improve outcomes. The evolution of robotic surgery has also led to new training programs. Surgeons undergo specialized training to master robotic systems, including simulation-based learning and hands-on practice.[33] This ensures the effective and safe use of robotic technology. Looking ahead, robotic surgery’s potential continues to expand. Emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, are expected to enhance robotic systems further, making them more intuitive and responsive.[34] These advancements promise to revolutionize surgical care, making procedures safer, less invasive, and more efficient. EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES IN SURGERY Impact of artificial intelligence in surgery AI is revolutionizing surgery by enhancing decision-making, improving precision, and optimizing patient outcomes. AI algorithms analyze vast data to assist in preoperative planning, intraoperative guidance, and postoperative care. For instance, AI-driven image recognition helps identify important anatomical structures and potential complications, reducing errors, and improving efficiency.[35] Machine learning, a subset of AI, predicts surgical outcomes, personalizes treatment plans, and assists in robotic surgeries. Supervised machine learning models analyze patient data to predict complications, enabling preventive measures.[34] AI integration into surgical practice promises more accurate, efficient, and personalized care. Augmented reality and virtual reality in surgical training and practice Augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) are transforming surgical training and practice by providing immersive, interactive, and realistic simulations. These technologies enable surgeons to practice complex procedures in a risk-free environment, enhancing skills and confidence.[36] AR overlays digital information onto the real world, helping surgeons visualize hidden structures such as blood vessels and tumors during surgery, thus improving precision and reducing complications. VR creates a fully immersive virtual environment for training and preoperative planning, allowing surgeons to simulate procedures and refine techniques.[37] As AR and VR technologies advance, their applications in surgery will expand, enhancing training and practice. Nanotechnology and bioprinting Nanotechnology and bioprinting are leading surgical innovations. Nanotechnology manipulates materials at the molecular level, enabling targeted drug delivery, imaging, and tissue repair. For instance, nanoparticles can deliver chemotherapy drugs directly to cancer cells, minimizing harm to healthy tissues.[38] Bioprinting, a form of 3D printing, creates complex biological structures such as tissues and organs layer by layer. This technology could revolutionize transplantation by providing custom-made, biocompatible organs. Researchers are making strides in printing tissues such as skin, cartilage, and heart parts.[39] As bioprinting advances, the potential for printing fully functional organs for transplantation becomes more realistic. CONCLUSION The journey of surgery from its humble beginnings to the modern era of robotic-assisted procedures showcases the advancements in medical science and technology. From the early rudimentary techniques to the transformative introduction of anesthesia and aseptic methods, surgery has continually evolved to improve patient outcomes. The advent of minimally invasive procedures through laparoscopy and endoscopy significantly reduced recovery times and complications. The integration of robotic systems has enabled surgeons to perform complex operations with greater precision and control. Looking ahead, emerging technologies such as AI, augmented and VR, nanotechnology, and bioprinting promise to further revolutionize surgical practice, making it safer, more efficient, and more effective. This evolution underscores the relentless pursuit of excellence in surgery, continuously enhancing patient care, and shaping the future of medical practice. Financial support and sponsorship Nil.
